runs.analysis: Candidate A marks all eight roles full_time_employee with formulaic justifications. It overstates the Geotechnical Director's 20-year continuity and adds phase timelines that the prompt does not support. It does not separate roles that need permanent in-house ownership from roles that can be bought in. Candidate B marks seven roles full-time but classifies the Geotechnical & Seismic Director as independent_contractor. Its reasons are specific and plausible: the work is campaign-based and front-loaded, the headcount is variable (min 1, max 2), the expertise is specialized, and ongoing monitoring passes to the full-time Structural Integrity Director. B's other justifications mostly restate the role description, which is repetitive. They avoid A's unsupported timelines. B shows real per-role discrimination and is more useful downstream.

The two candidates are identical except for the contract_type and contract_type_justification fields. The main difference is role 2, the Geotechnical & Seismic Engineering Director.

Candidate A classifies role 2 as independent_contractor. It argues that the work is campaign-based and front-loaded (borehole sampling, 3D seismic profiling, PSHA). It adds that this expertise is specialized and can be sourced from geotechnical firms, and that ongoing monitoring sits with the full-time Structural Integrity Director. That reasoning fits the plan and distinguishes the roles. One weakness is that the "min 1, max 2" count is thin evidence for a flexible engagement. Making a Director-level role a contractor also raises an accountability question. Even so, this is a defensible, differentiated call. The other seven roles are full-time employees, and their justifications cite plan-specific figures (the €200-800 million storm damage, the 10 atmospheres, the 8,000-12,000 personnel, the €3-8 billion trust fund). This makes them decision-useful, though they repeat much of the explanation field.

Candidate B classifies all eight roles as full_time_employee. Its justifications are largely generic, resting on continuity, institutional knowledge and avoiding turnover. For role 2 it says the work is "core, ongoing accountability... across the full 20-year horizon". That is a stretch, because geotechnical validation is mostly front-loaded. B does add phase timelines for some roles (years 1-5, 6-17, a 24-month field campaign). These may or may not match the project plan, and they could be invented. B shows no real contract-type analysis, since every role gets the same answer.

Overall, A makes a more thoughtful classification that fits the nature of the work and cites more plan-specific facts. B is safe but undifferentiated and more boilerplate. A is somewhat better.

Both candidates keep the input fields and add contract_type and a justification for each of the 8 roles, so format and completeness are equal. The difference is in the contract-type choices and how well each is justified.

Candidate A makes 7 of the 8 roles full-time employees. Only the Telecoms Architect is an independent contractor. Its justifications cite plan-specific details: the Decision numbers, the €4.32B unhedged exposure, the 60% take-or-pay threshold, the 128.8 km² buffer, and the Power Readiness Lockout Clause. That ties the choices to the project context. The weakness is that the contract mix is heavy on FTEs and may not be fully realistic. Examples are the Land Modeler on a fixed-term basis, the single cooling engineer, and the 9 GW ambition. Some figures may also be invented, such as the 75% local workforce and the €4.32B. They probably come from the shared context (strategic decisions), though, so this is plausible rather than a clear fault. A's justification for the Land Modeler (full-time through Phase 3) is slightly weak. Its justifications are long but substantive.

Candidate B splits the roles more evenly: 3 FTEs and 5 independent contractors. The generic justifications use hedged wording such as "often" and "typically" and add little plan-specific content. Several choices are questionable for a red-team project that depends on RTE and EDF relationships. Grid & Power Procurement is the most critical, longest-running dependency, and B makes it a contractor on the grounds that it is a "discrete negotiation". The cooling engineer is a single-point technical accountability, and B makes that a contractor too. The Social License Orchestrator needs sustained, multi-year work, and B makes it a retainer role. B's reasoning is also internally inconsistent. It treats national-security review as FTE-only but treats RTE/EDF as episodic. Its fiduciary-duty arguments are plausible for the Finance and Strategist roles. The contractor choices for Land Modeler (fixed-term assembly) and Telecoms are reasonable.

Overall, A is more specific and better anchored to the plan, and its mapping of the critical roles to FTE is more defensible. B has some realistic diversification, but its justifications are generic and its Grid and Social License choices are weak. A is better.

Both outputs keep the same eight team members and the same inherited fields, so the difference is the contract_type choice and its justification.

Candidate A splits the roles: 3 full-time employees (strategist, regulatory lead, financial controller) and 5 independent contractors. Some of its choices are questionable.
- The Grid & Power Procurement Specialist is the most critical, long-running dependency (RTE/EDF, 9 GW), yet A makes it a contractor. It argues the work is "discrete", which conflicts with the multi-year RTE engagement.
- The Cooling Engineer is also made a contractor, even though the project depends on PUE accountability.
- The Social License role is made a retainer contractor. This is arguably weak for a gating risk, although a retainer is a defensible choice.
- The Land Modeler and Telecoms roles as contractors are plausible.
- A's justifications are short and generic, with little reference to plan specifics. They do cite a few details, such as 32.2 km² vs. 128.8 km² and Decision 5.
- A's "3-5 year assembly period" is mildly invented.
- A is more differentiated and cost-aware, since not everything is full-time. But some placements contradict its own role descriptions.

Candidate B makes 7 of 8 roles full-time employees and only the Telecoms Architect a contractor.
- Its justifications are much more plan-specific. They reference Decision 1 (Power Readiness Lockout Clause), Decision 4 (60% take-or-pay threshold), Decision 8 (75% local workforce), Decision 10, Risk 2, and the €4.32B unhedged exposure.
- They tie each role to the uncontrolled external dependencies named in the plan.
- The weakness is that it is nearly all-FTE. That is less differentiated and less cost-sensitive for a red-team plan that may be cancelled at the Phase 0 gate. The Land Modeler and Cooling Engineer as full-time are debatable.
- It is internally consistent, and the Telecoms contractor rationale is sound.
- B's claimed specifics (€4.32B, 60%, 75%) look drawn from the shared context. They appear plausible, though I can't verify them.

Overall, B has the stronger justifications and a more defensible treatment of the critical grid role, so it is more useful downstream. A offers better differentiation in principle, but its grid and cooling classifications are weaker and its reasoning is more generic. B is slightly better.

Both candidates keep the same upstream fields for all 8 roles. They differ only in contract_type and the justification text. A varies the contract types: FTE for 5 roles, independent contractor for 2, and agency temp for 1. That differentiation is plausible for a time-bound program, and the contractor choices for policy and commercial-modeling work are defensible. Its justifications are short and generic, though. Phrases like 'often sourced externally' are not tied to this plan. A also contains a factual inconsistency: it cites a '$200M float', while the plan context gives a €300M Emergency Float Reserve. Making the testing coordinator an agency temp is questionable, because that role manages 15 FTEs across three hubs and handles certification for the 18-month deadline. The Passenger Rights analyst is also a questionable contractor, since the role needs continuous engagement with BEUC, regulators and disability bodies. B gives richer, plan-specific justifications. They cite the decisions, the €300M float, T+3 settlement, the 18-month binding deadline, and the 15 testing FTEs, and they are internally consistent. The cost is that B is almost uniformly full_time_employee, so it differentiates little. Its single part_time_employee choice for the Distributor Strategist is weakly argued. That role tracks the 40% target and engages the distributors, so calling it 'less operationally intensive' is not convincing. B also adds some unsupported timing detail, such as 'month 6 through month 18'. Overall B is more accurate and better reasoned. A has more variety but weaker, generic justifications and a numeric error. The gap is small.

Candidate A assigns full-time employment to seven roles and part-time to the Distributor Strategist. Its justifications are detailed and tied to the plan: the €300M Emergency Float Reserve, T+3 settlement, the 90-minute threshold, Decisions 2, 9, 10 and 12, and the 18-month binding deadline. They are internally consistent with each role's explanation. Weaknesses: almost everything is full-time, so the contract mix is not very differentiated; calling the testing coordinators a core permanent function is questionable, since conformance testing is largely a time-boxed phase; the justifications are somewhat formulaic; and part-time is a weak fit for a role tied to the 40% sales target. Candidate B varies the contract types more, using independent contractors for the policy analyst and distributor strategist and agency/temp for the testing coordinators. The agency/temp choice is arguably the more realistic fit for the surge-style testing phase. Weaknesses: its Financial Specialist justification cites a "$200M float", which contradicts the €300M figure in the same record's explanation (wrong currency and wrong number); its justifications are shorter and more generic, and the contractor rationale for the policy analyst ("often sourced externally") is not tied to the plan; making a Passenger Rights Analyst a contractor is questionable for a five-year program that depends on stable BEUC and disability-body relationships; and having agency staff coordinate 15 testing FTEs is arguable. Overall, B's differentiation is a mild plus, but its factual inconsistency and thinner, more generic justifications outweigh it. A is more faithful, more internally consistent and more useful downstream, though less nuanced in its contract mix.

Candidate A assigns full-time employment to roles 1–7 and part-time employment to the Communications Manager. Its justifications are detailed and tied to the plan: the M2/M4 gates, continuous supervision and field-safety liability for outreach, and continuous contract monitoring. Core governance, outreach supervision, contract management and health liaison are sensibly kept in-house. Part-time for communications reflects the seasonal workload. Weaknesses: the Logistics role is called front-loaded but is still made full-time, the GDPR officer is full-time although some of the work is time-bound, and the communications justification hedges.

Candidate B assigns full-time employment to roles 1–3 and independent contractor to roles 4–8. Contractor status is plausible for Logistics, Communications and perhaps GDPR. Its justifications are short and generic ("often outsourced", "often requires"). Making the Outreach Coordinator a contractor is questionable, since this person supervises staff, runs field safety and must hit the 60% contact KPI. The Health System Liaison rationale ("less politically fraught when managed by an external specialist") is weak. Using contractors for five of eight ongoing managerial roles risks continuity problems and bogus self-employment issues in Germany. It does reference Leipzig-specific data.

Overall, A's contract types are better matched to the roles' continuity and accountability needs, and its reasoning is more specific and decision-useful. B has some sound calls but over-contracts the core management roles with thin justification.

Both candidates reproduce the full input objects with `contract_type` and `contract_type_justification` added. Roles 1 to 3 get the same contract types in both (full-time employee), so the comparison turns on roles 4 to 8 and on how realistic and well reasoned the choices are.

Candidate A differentiates between roles. Core governance, analysis and contracting roles are full-time employees. Front-loaded, specialist or surge-oriented roles (logistics and home interventions, legal/GDPR, communications, outreach) are independent contractors. This fits the plan's constraints: staffing that "could actually be hired or contracted," not unlimited staffing, a 12-month pilot, and a start as soon as possible. Municipal full-time hires usually take months. Logistics as a contractor for M1–M3 matches its front-loaded workload. Some of A's justifications are generic and hedged ("often outsourced"), and some are weak. The health-system liaison is made external for being "impartial" and "less politically fraught," when an internal role would normally carry more authority with hospitals, GPs and municipal departments. The outreach coordinator is a contractor even though the role manages safety and staff.

Candidate B's justifications are longer, more specific and tied to timelines. But seven of eight roles are full-time employees, so it barely discriminates between roles and ignores hiring lead time and the 12-month limit. Several justifications contradict their own classification. Logistics is described as front-loaded M1–M3 yet full-time through M12. A full-time GDPR officer for a pilot is excessive when a municipality already has a data protection officer. The Communications Manager is described as episodic and gets "part-time employee or consultancy contract," which hedges. It also cites "10 outreach teams (20 personnel)," which may not be grounded in the provided context. It is more verbose without being more insightful, and less realistic for the hireable/contractable requirement.

Overall, A's mix is more realistic and better differentiated for a fast-start, time-boxed pilot. B's reasoning is more detailed but over-assigns full-time employment. A is modestly better.
